blocks.content: Picture keeping two versions of your notes for a class. One is the messy notebook where you scribble everything the second you hear it, half in shorthand, in whatever order it came to you.
The other is a clean, retyped set of notes you make later, organized by topic, easy to search, easy to trust.
Both are useful. The messy notebook has everything, even the stuff you didn't think mattered yet. The clean version is what you actually study from before an exam.

Now imagine keeping both of them up to date, forever, by hand. Every time something changes in the messy notebook, someone has to remember to go update the clean copy too. Miss an update and the two stop agreeing with each other.

That's basically the problem a data lakehouse showed up to fix. The messy notebook is a data lake. The clean copy is a data warehouse. And keeping them in sync by hand is exactly as annoying as it sounds.
1. Introduction

A data lakehouse takes the cheap, flexible storage of a data lake and adds a transactional, warehouse like layer directly on top of it. Instead of running a lake and a warehouse as two separate systems that you keep in sync yourself, you end up with one copy of the data that behaves like both, depending on who's asking.

This lesson walks through why teams got stuck maintaining two systems in the first place, what a lakehouse actually bolts on to fix that, the technologies that make it real, and where the pattern still falls short of a dedicated warehouse.

blocks.title: What you'll walk away with
blocks.content: Why a lake and a warehouse used to be run as separate systems, what a lakehouse's transactional layer actually adds, how Delta Lake and Iceberg approach this conceptually, what you genuinely give up by choosing a lakehouse, who's using this in production today, and how to bring this up in a system design interview.
2. The Problem: Two Separate Systems
2.1 A lake for raw data, a warehouse for fast queries
blocks.text: 2.1 A lake for raw data, a warehouse for fast queries

blocks.content: Before the lakehouse pattern existed, a typical company ran two storage systems side by side. Raw events, logs, and unstructured files landed in a data lake, usually cheap object storage like S3, because it was flexible and inexpensive.

Anything an analyst wanted to slice with a dashboard or a fast SQL query lived in a separate data warehouse, like Redshift, Snowflake, or BigQuery, where the schema was fixed and query performance was tuned for exactly that kind of workload.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396341725-336141404.png
blocks.alt: A data lake feeding a nightly ETL job that copies data into a separate data warehouse, creating a stale second copy

blocks.content: 2.2 Two copies, duplicated storage, and staleness
blocks.text: 2.2 Two copies, duplicated storage, and staleness

blocks.content: Running both systems meant running a pipeline between them too. A scheduled job pulled data out of the lake, cleaned and reshaped it, and loaded it into the warehouse, usually once a night.

That meant paying to store the same data twice, maintaining a pipeline whose only job was reformatting, and living with a staleness window between the two copies. If that nightly job failed or ran late, the warehouse showed yesterday's numbers while the lake already had today's.

blocks.title: The gotcha
blocks.content: The dashboard says one number, the lake says another, and nobody on the team is fully sure which one is currently true. That drift is the real cost of running two copies of the same data, not just the extra storage bill.
3. The Core Idea: A Transactional Layer on Cheap Storage
blocks.text: 3. The Core Idea: A Transactional Layer on Cheap Storage

blocks.content: A lakehouse's core idea is simple to state: keep the data exactly where it already lives, in cheap object storage, and add a table format layer on top that tracks schema, versions, and which files currently belong to a table. Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, and Apache Hudi are the three projects that implement this idea.
3.1 A metadata layer sits on top of object storage
blocks.text: 3.1 A metadata layer sits on top of object storage

blocks.content: Underneath, nothing changes. Your data is still Parquet files sitting in S3 or a similar object store, just as cheap as before. What's new is a layer of metadata that wraps those files: a manifest of which files make up the table right now, what their columns and types are, and a history of every change ever committed.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396341726-163858273.png
blocks.alt: A transactional metadata layer sitting between raw object storage and both SQL queries and ML training jobs

blocks.content: 3.2 ACID transactions on lake files

Raw object storage was never built with transactions in mind. If two jobs wrote to the same location at once, a reader could see a half finished write, duplicate rows, or a mix of old and new files with no way to tell which version was correct.

The metadata layer fixes this by making every change an atomic commit. A reader either sees the complete result of a write or none of it at all, the same guarantee you'd expect from a database, now applied to files sitting in a lake.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396341727-46896750.png
blocks.alt: Two concurrent writers committing to the same table, with the metadata layer producing one consistent snapshot for readers

blocks.content: 3.3 Schema enforcement
A raw data lake famously accepts anything. A field renamed, a type flipped from an integer to a string, none of it gets caught until something downstream quietly breaks.

A lakehouse table tracks an actual schema and can reject a write the moment it doesn't match. That single check is what makes a lakehouse table trustworthy enough for a BI dashboard to depend on directly.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396343744-797704329.png
blocks.alt: An incoming record being checked against a table's schema, accepted when it matches and rejected when it doesn't

blocks.content: 3.4 Time travel
Because every change is a tracked, versioned commit, you can ask the table what it looked like at an earlier point, not just what it looks like right now. This is called time travel.

It's genuinely useful in practice: reproduce the exact training set an ML model was trained on months ago, or roll a query back to the version right before someone accidentally overwrote good data with a bad batch job.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396343746-368029668.png
blocks.alt: A table's version history with a time travel query reading an earlier version instead of the current one

blocks.content:
SELECT * FROM sales_events VERSION AS OF 42;

SELECT * FROM sales_events TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-06-01 00:00:00';

SELECT * FROM sales_events TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-06-01 00:00:00';

blocks.content: 4. Key Technologies

Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, and Apache Hudi all implement roughly the same idea, a table format layer over object storage, with different internal mechanics. You don't need their implementation details memorized, just the conceptual shape of how each one tracks table state.
4.1 Delta Lake's transaction log

Delta Lake, created by Databricks, tracks every change to a table as an ordered sequence of JSON entries called the transaction log, stored right alongside the data files in a folder named _delta_log. Each entry records exactly which files were added or removed by that commit.
Reading the table means replaying that log to figure out the current set of valid files. Reading an old version just means replaying the log only up to that point.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396343746-285952074.png
blocks.alt: A sequence of commits building up Delta Lake's transaction log, which readers replay to know the table's current files

blocks.content: 4.2 Apache Iceberg's snapshots

Apache Iceberg takes a slightly different approach built around snapshots. Every change to the table produces a brand new snapshot, a pointer to the exact set of data files valid at that moment, connected through a chain of manifest files.
A query engine picks a snapshot, most often the newest one, and reads only the files it points to. Older snapshots stay around, which is what makes Iceberg's time travel and rollback features work.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396343746-885005827.png
blocks.alt: A chain of Iceberg table snapshots with a query engine picking the current snapshot to read from

blocks.content: Apache Hudi solves a similar problem with a stronger focus on fast upserts and streaming ingestion, which is why it shows up most often in pipelines with constant incremental updates rather than pure batch loads.
5. What a Lakehouse Unlocks
5.1 One copy of data for both worlds
blocks.text: 5.1 One copy of data for both worlds

blocks.content: With ACID guarantees and a real schema sitting on top of the lake, the same table can now serve two very different audiences. A data scientist can point Spark at it and pull every raw column for model training. An analyst can point a BI tool at the exact same table and run fast, filtered aggregate queries.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396343747-944708866.png
blocks.alt: One set of Parquet files serving both a Spark ML training job and a BI dashboard directly

blocks.content: 5.2 No more lake-to-warehouse ETL just for analytics
blocks.text: 5.2 No more lake-to-warehouse ETL just for analytics

blocks.content: The pipeline whose only job was reshaping lake data into a warehouse friendly format stops being necessary. If the lake table already has a schema, already supports transactions, and already performs well enough for structured queries, there's nothing left for that ETL job to produce.

6. Trade-offs
6.1 A newer, still maturing ecosystem

A lakehouse is a genuinely newer pattern than either a pure lake or a pure warehouse, and it shows. Tooling, connectors, and BI integrations are still catching up compared to decades old warehouse engines.

There's also an active format war between Delta Lake, Iceberg, and Hudi. Picking one is closer to picking a database engine than picking a file format, and migrating a large table between formats later is not a small job.

blocks.title: Worth knowing
blocks.content: Choosing a table format is a long term commitment for a team, not a detail to decide casually. Which engines and BI tools your organization already uses often matters more than which format is technically newest.
6.2 Query performance can still lag a dedicated warehouse
blocks.text: 6.2 Query performance can still lag a dedicated warehouse

blocks.content: For the most demanding BI workloads, dashboards hit by hundreds of concurrent users expecting sub second responses, a purpose built warehouse engine with its own proprietary storage format and aggressive caching can still outperform a lakehouse query engine reading open Parquet files.
A lakehouse closes most of that gap, but for extreme concurrency or extreme latency requirements, a dedicated warehouse is still the safer choice.

7. Real World Adoption
7.1 Databricks and Delta Lake

Databricks pioneered and popularized the lakehouse pattern, building Delta Lake as an open source table format and pushing the term itself into the industry's vocabulary. Most conversations about lakehouses trace back to Databricks' original pitch: stop maintaining two systems.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396343747-540380907.png
blocks.alt: Databricks, Snowflake, and BigQuery all converging on lakehouse style patterns from different starting points

blocks.content: 7.2 Snowflake and BigQuery adding lakehouse style support
blocks.text: 7.2 Snowflake and BigQuery adding lakehouse style support

blocks.content: Warehouse vendors responded by meeting the lakehouse pattern halfway. Snowflake added support for querying Iceberg tables directly, letting data stay in a customer's own object storage instead of being loaded into Snowflake's proprietary format.
BigQuery added BigLake and external table support for the same reason, letting its query engine read Iceberg or Delta tables sitting in cloud storage as if they were native BigQuery tables.
8. Worked Example: One Set of Parquet Files, Two Workloads
blocks.text: 8. Worked Example: One Set of Parquet Files, Two Workloads

blocks.title: The scenario
blocks.text: A company stores its order events as Parquet files in an S3 bucket, managed by Delta Lake. There is no separate warehouse copy. A Spark job trains a fraud detection model against the same files a BI dashboard queries every morning.

blocks.content: 8.1 The setup
The Parquet files themselves never move. What makes them queryable as a proper table is the Delta Lake transaction log sitting next to them, tracking schema and every commit made to the data.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396343747-167036214.png
blocks.alt: S3 Parquet files managed by Delta Lake, queried by both a Spark training job and a BI tool with no separate warehouse copy

blocks.content: 8.2 A Spark ML training job reads the table
blocks.text: 8.2 A Spark ML training job reads the table

blocks.content: The data science team reads the full table directly with Spark, pulling every raw column, including ones the BI dashboard never touches, to build a training set for a fraud model.

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("fraud-training").getOrCreate()

orders = spark.read.format("delta").load("s3://company-lakehouse/orders")
training_set = orders.select(
    "order_id", "user_id", "amount", "device_fingerprint", "ip_country", "is_fraud"
)
training_set.write.format("parquet").save("s3://company-ml/fraud-training-set")

blocks.content: 8.3 A BI tool queries the very same table
blocks.text: 8.3 A BI tool queries the very same table

blocks.content: At the same time, a BI dashboard connects to the exact same Delta table through Spark SQL and runs a simple aggregate query for a daily revenue chart. Same files, same transaction log, no separate warehouse copy sitting somewhere else waiting to go stale.

SELECT DATE(order_ts) AS day, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM delta.`s3://company-lakehouse/orders`
GROUP BY DATE(order_ts)
ORDER BY day DESC
LIMIT 30;

blocks.content: 9. Implementation Walkthrough
9.1 Writing a Delta Lake table with Spark
blocks.text: 9.1 Writing a Delta Lake table with Spark

blocks.content: Creating a Delta table from a dataframe is close to writing any other file format, the format name is really the only difference. Delta Lake sets up the transaction log for you the first time you write.

orders_df.write.format("delta").mode("append").save("s3://company-lakehouse/orders")

# Reading it back later is just as plain
orders = spark.read.format("delta").load("s3://company-lakehouse/orders")
orders.show(5)

blocks.content: 9.2 Time travel query in practice
Because Delta Lake keeps every commit, you can ask for the table as it looked several versions ago, useful when you need to check what changed or recover from a bad write.

history_df = spark.sql("DESCRIBE HISTORY delta.`s3://company-lakehouse/orders`")
history_df.select("version", "timestamp", "operation").show()

old_orders = spark.read.format("delta").option("versionAsOf", 17).load("s3://company-lakehouse/orders")

blocks.content: 9.3 Schema enforcement blocking a bad write
blocks.text: 9.3 Schema enforcement blocking a bad write

blocks.content: If a job tries to write a dataframe whose columns don't match the table's existing schema, Delta Lake rejects the write outright instead of silently corrupting the table.

bad_df = spark.createDataFrame([("o1", "not_a_number")], ["order_id", "amount"])

# amount is expected to be numeric, this write fails with an AnalysisException
bad_df.write.format("delta").mode("append").save("s3://company-lakehouse/orders")

code.content:
bad_df = spark.createDataFrame([("o1", "not_a_number")], ["order_id", "amount"])

# amount is expected to be numeric, this write fails with an AnalysisException
bad_df.write.format("delta").mode("append").save("s3://company-lakehouse/orders")

bad_df.write.format("delta").mode("append").save("s3://company-lakehouse/orders")

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.content: That failed write is the entire point. In a raw lake with no schema enforcement, this bad record would have landed quietly and broken a dashboard or a training run days later, with nobody sure why.
10. Interview Angle

When an interviewer asks how you'd avoid running both a data lake and a data warehouse for the same data, a lakehouse is a strong, current answer, as long as you can explain what it actually buys you and where it still falls short.

blocks.title: Don't stop at the pitch
blocks.content: Mentioning a lakehouse and stopping there sounds like a buzzword. Following it up with the actual trade-offs is what tells an interviewer you understand the pattern instead of just recognizing the name.
A lakehouse isn't magic, it's a transaction log doing the boring, unglamorous work of making a pile of files behave like a database table.
